structure.title: Acts I–II · Two copies of a love letter
structure.text: Falstaff hopes to improve his finances by courting two prosperous wives. He economises on the writing, and the women compare notes. Before he has had a chance to play the lover, the two people he expected to deceive are arranging his entrances and exits for him.

structure.title: Acts III–IV · Getting a visitor out of a house
structure.text: The wives have a practical problem each time Falstaff arrives. Ford may burst in, the servants have their jobs to do, and a large knight needs somewhere to go. Meanwhile, the Pages are considering husbands for their daughter Anne. Several people in Windsor have mistaken the ability to arrange a meeting for the ability to determine what a woman will choose.

structure.title: Act V · Windsor stages its own ghost story
structure.text: The park gives the plotters more room and a local legend gives them the costumes. Different parties give different instructions about whom to meet in the dark. The fun comes partly from knowing that each adult thinks a disguise will make their own plan wonderfully simple.

people.name: Mistress Page and Mistress Ford
people.text: Each woman could have spent an uncomfortable afternoon wondering what a knight meant by his attentions. Meeting each other changes the situation instantly. The wives can turn Falstaff's letters into comedy because each trusts the other with a piece of information that a jealous husband might treat very differently.

people.name: Falstaff and Ford
people.role: A penniless schemer and a paying customer
people.text: Ford assumes a false name to hire Falstaff to court Mistress Ford. He hopes to discover the truth about his wife from a man he is paying to deceive her. Falstaff has excellent financial reasons to make his client believe that the seduction is going splendidly.

people.name: Anne Page
people.role: A daughter whose parents favour different suitors
people.text: The Pages are perfectly capable of seeing through Falstaff's vanity. They find it harder to see that their daughter has preferences of her own. Anne's courtship gives the household comedy a second generation of people with reasons to keep a secret.

context.title: A town small enough to share a joke
context.text: The Garter Inn, two households and the park are close enough for news and costumes to travel quickly. People know one another's trades, habits and ways of talking. That familiarity makes it possible both to recognise a disguise and to cooperate in a performance elaborate enough to fool a neighbour.

notice.text: Notice what the laundry basket means to each visitor.
notice.why: To the servants it is something to carry. To the wives it offers a way through the next few minutes. Ford sees a room he must search. A stage full of people can look at the same piece of household equipment and inhabit three entirely different versions of the scene.

passages.quote: take this basket on your shoulders

notice.text: Listen for the extra flourish in Falstaff's account to the disguised Ford.
notice.why: He is describing a prospective conquest to someone who wants both to finance and to prevent it. The more confidence his story inspires in the paying customer, the more determined the husband becomes to catch him. Both listeners occupy the same chair.

opening: Falstaff decides to improve his finances by seducing two married women who can access their husbands' money. He economises on effort by sending them nearly identical letters. Unfortunately for him, the women compare notes and find the proposal more useful as entertainment than temptation. Shakespeare brings his great opportunist into a town where household intelligence can defeat swagger, while a jealous husband supplies additional confusion. The comedy belongs to people who understand exactly how they are being underestimated and decide to make the experience expensive.
